text: The name hydrogen comes from Greek words meaning "water" and "forming", because it burned in air to form water.
Hydrogen was discovered by the English physicist Henry Cavendish.
Written records indicate that Robert Boyle produced hydrogen gas as early as 1671 while experimenting with iron and acids.
Hydrogen is used for filling balloons.
Hydrogen is added to fats and oils, such as peanut oil, through a process called hydrogenation.
The hydrogen fuel cell is a developing technology for obtaining electrical power from hydrogen gas.
Liquid hydrogen is used in the study of superconductors.
Carbon has been known since ancient times.
The name carbon comes from the Latin word carbo, meaning "charcoal".
Carbon was known in prehistoric times in the form of charcoal and soot.
In 1797, the English chemist Smithson Tennant proved that diamond is pure carbon.
The black material in pencils, often called lead, is actually graphite.
Carbon black, a kind of black soot, is used to make inks, paints and rubber products.
Graphite, a form of carbon, is mainly used as a lubricant.
A radioactive isotope of carbon is used to find the age of formerly living things, through a process known as radiocarbon dating.
Nitrogen was discovered or first isolated in 1772.
Nitrogen was discovered by the Scottish physician and chemist Daniel Rutherford in 1772.
The name nitrogen comes from words meaning "native soda" and "forming".
Rutherford removed oxygen and carbon dioxide from air and showed that the remaining gas would not support burning or living things.
The largest use of nitrogen is for making ammonia.
Liquid nitrogen is used for refrigeration.
Liquid nitrogen is used to preserve biological samples.
Nitrogen gas is used as a protective shield in the semiconductor industry.
The name oxygen comes from Greek words meaning "acid" and "forming".
The name oxygen was created by Antoine Lavoisier, who incorrectly believed that oxygen was necessary to form all acids.
Joseph Priestley and Carl Wilhelm Scheele both discovered oxygen independently, but Priestley is usually given credit for the discovery.
Plants and animals rely on oxygen for respiration.
Hospitals frequently prescribe oxygen for patients with breathing illnesses.
Oxygen is used in making steel, where it burns away impurities in molten iron.
Oxygen can be combined with acetylene to produce a very hot flame used for welding.
Sodium was discovered or first isolated in 1807.
Sodium was discovered in 1807 by the English chemist Humphry Davy.
The name sodium comes from the English word soda and the Latin sodanum, meaning "headache remedy".
The symbol Na comes from the Latin word natrium.
Sodium vapor is used in streetlights and produces a brilliant yellow light.
Sodium forms many useful compounds, including table salt and baking soda.
Liquid sodium has been used as a coolant for nuclear reactors.
Sodium is used in the production of titanium.
The name magnesium comes from Magnesia, a district in the north-eastern region of Greece called Thessalia.
The Scottish chemist Joseph Black recognized magnesium as a separate element in 1755.
In 1808, the English chemist Humphry Davy obtained impure magnesium metal.
Cameras, horseshoes, baseball catchers' masks and snowshoes are among the items made from magnesium alloys.
Magnesium oxide is used in some antacids.
A thin film of magnesium fluoride is applied to optical lenses to help reduce glare and reflections.
Magnesium carbonate is added to table salt to prevent caking.
Chlorine was discovered or first isolated in 1774.
The name chlorine comes from the Greek word chloros, meaning "pale green" or "greenish yellow".
Chlorine was discovered by the Swedish pharmacist and chemist Carl-Wilhelm Scheele in 1774.
In 1810, the English chemist Humphry Davy proved that chlorine was an element.
Chlorine is used to make drinking water safe and to treat swimming pools.
Chlorine is commonly used as an antiseptic.
Sodium chloride, a chlorine compound commonly known as table salt, is used to season food.
Chlorine is used in the production of paper products, textiles and medicines.
Iron has been known since ancient times.
The name iron comes from an Anglo-Saxon word of unknown origin.
The symbol Fe comes from the Latin word ferrum, meaning "firmness".
Iron is mentioned many times in the Old Testament of the Bible.
Huge amounts of iron are used to make steel, an alloy of iron and carbon.
Steel is used to make paper clips, skyscrapers and everything in between.
Adding chromium to steel improves its durability and prevents rust, making stainless steel.
Iron sulfate is used to treat the blood disease anemia.
Copper has been known since ancient times.
The name copper comes from the Latin cuprum, for Cyprus, the island where the Romans first obtained copper.
The symbol Cu also comes from the Latin cuprum.
Copper has been known since prehistoric times.
The electrical industry uses copper in the form of wire.
Since it resists corrosion from the air, moisture and seawater, copper has been widely used in coins.
Copper is used to make water pipes and jewelry.
Brass, an alloy of copper, is used today in some musical instruments and screws.
Gold has been known since ancient times.
The name gold comes from the Sanskrit word jval, meaning "shine", and the Teutonic word gulth, meaning "shining metal".
The symbol Au comes from the Latin aurum, for Aurora, the goddess of dawn.
Gold was known and highly valued in prehistoric times.
Gold alloys are used to make jewelry, decorative items, dental fillings and coins.
Thin sheets of gold, known as gold leaf, are mainly used in arts and crafts for gilding.
Gold can be used to make electrical connectors and printed circuit boards.
Gold is used for coating certain space satellites, as it is a good reflector of infrared and is inert.
The atomic number is the number of protons in the nucleus. It is what makes an element that element.
A neutral atom has the same number of electrons as protons.
The mass number counts protons and neutrons together, so neutrons = mass number − atomic number.
Isotopes are atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons.
Orbitals that have the same principal quantum number form a shell, and each shell is divided into subshells.
Valence electrons are the electrons in the highest-numbered shell, plus any in the last unfilled subshell. They largely control an atom's chemistry.
